facts.text: Cinematographer Jan de Bont shot this as his American debut. He later directed the blockbusters Speed and Twister.
Eric Brown, who plays Philly, first auditioned for the smaller part of Philly's best friend Sherman (Patrick Piccininni), the boy on screen now, and ended up the lead.
Future Wayne's World star Dana Carvey did voiceover work on the film's US trailer and TV ads.
The film was financed by Barry & Enright Productions, the team behind TV game shows. Their staff announcer, Jay Stewart, narrated the trailer.
Howard Hesseman, the chauffeur Lester, was radio DJ Dr. Johnny Fever on WKRP in Cincinnati. He wore a wig and mustache here.
Pamela Bryant, who plays Philly's sister Joyce, also appeared in the slasher Don't Answer the Phone!
Game-show host and producer Jack Barry reportedly got a pile of hate mail from his TV fans over this movie, and he never made another film.
Sylvia Kristel, who plays the French housekeeper Nicole Mallow, is actually Dutch. She became famous in the Emmanuelle films.
This was the first release of Jensen Farley Pictures, a new offshoot of family-film maker Sunn Classic. The company later put out the sex comedy Homework, with Joan Collins.
Universal and other distributors passed on the film. After it tested well in selected markets, brand-new Jensen Farley Pictures finally picked it up.
The film is based on Philly, a 1969 novel by Dan Greenburg. Universal optioned it twice in the 60s and 70s, then dropped it. Greenburg wrote this screenplay himself.
The film licensed hits by Rod Stewart (three songs), Eric Clapton, Air Supply, Earth, Wind & Fire and John Cougar, all on a budget of only about $3 million.
Sylvia Kristel didn't do all her own nude scenes. Judy Helden, credited as 'Miss Kristel's Double', stood in for the striptease.
Eric Brown wasn't the first Philly. Another actor was fired after 18 days of shooting, and Brown, a stage kid, took over the lead.
Ed Begley Jr., the tennis coach Jack Travis, soon became Dr. Ehrlich on St. Elsewhere. He and Howard Hesseman reunited in This Is Spinal Tap.
Eric Brown, who plays Philly, later played Ken Berry's son on the first seasons of the sitcom Mama's Family, spun off from The Carol Burnett Show.
The UK censor, the BBFC, cut 3 minutes 20 seconds, mostly shots of a nude Sylvia Kristel with the teenage actor, gutting the bath scene. Britain still gets the cut version.
For US TV airings the bath scene was removed by changing one line: Philly answers 'No' to the invitation and the scene just ends.
It opened August 28, 1981 in 134 theaters and ranked 9th that weekend with $1.18 million. The Numbers tallies $18.1 million total, well under the $26 million often quoted.
Screenwriter Dan Greenburg also wrote Kiss My Firm But Pliant Lips, the book behind the Elvis Presley film Live a Little, Love a Little.
Critic Donald Guarisco on Schlockmania called it 'a mess that manages to be daring and lame all at once,' and 'clean-scrubbed smut.'
Made for about $2.8 million, the film grossed roughly $26 million. Leonard Maltin called it a 'surprise box-office hit'.
Director Alan Myerson co-founded the improv troupe The Committee, as did Howard Hesseman (Lester). Myerson also played O.K. Corrales in Billy Jack.
The film is part of an early-80s cycle of older-woman/younger-man movies set off by the Canadian hit In Praise of Older Women. Others: Class and My Tutor.
Sylvia Kristel said in 2006 that she'd owned a share of the film but sold it to her manager for $150,000, missing out on its big box-office take.
Vision Features filed a $15 million lawsuit against Barry & Enright and producer R. Ben Efraim in 1981, claiming unpaid fees and lack of proper credit.
After a rough cut in summer 1980, the producers had new scenes shot to emphasize the seduction over the blackmail plot. About 20 minutes of the finished film was reshot.
James Fargo directed uncredited extra footage. He directed The Enforcer, the third Dirty Harry film, which is why the film is namechecking it right now.
Vince Leo of Qwipster's Movie Reviews gave the film 2 out of 5 stars, calling it 'subpar stuff on almost any other level' while praising Sylvia Kristel's sexiness.
The motel manager is screenwriter Dan Greenburg, who wrote the novel Philly that the film is based on.
Italy made its own remake in the mid-80s, Il peccato di Lola (Lola's Sin), starring Donatella Damiani.
The film had legs: The Numbers ranks it 6th at the box office on the weekends of September 11 and November 20, 1981, nearly three months after it opened.
In Australia the film was banned for cinema and video and then cut by 10+ minutes for an R rating over the sexual exploitation of a minor.
Sylvia Kristel's cameo in 1983's Private School was reportedly a contractual obligation to this film's producers.
Private Lessons II (1993) was a Japanese production. Qwipster's Vince Leo calls it a sequel in name only, more of a remake.
The school sign reads 'Fredrick Douglass High School', misspelling the abolitionist Frederick Douglass.
Producer R. Ben Efraim made two in-name-only sequels, Private Lessons II (1993) and Private Lessons: Another Story (1994), plus Private School and Private Resort.
